article_title: The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence
citation: Marciano Laura, Camerini Anne-Linda, Morese Rosalba. (2021). The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.671817
title: I-PACE model of addictive online behaviors
description: The review summarizes the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model (Brand et al., 2016, 2019), in which "cognition, personality, existing psychopathology, and motivations determine how people use the Internet in a specific way." Early online behaviors provide gratifications and relief from negative moods, creating reward expectancies; repetitive checking and obtained gratifications act as reinforcement, and conditioning processes lead to compulsive use. The imbalance between growing gratifying-oriented urges and diminishing inhibitory control is pivotal for developing online behavioral addictions.
requirements: Cognitive and affective response to Internet use together with obtained gratifications fostering subsequent use
constraints: The review notes the type of environment (online versus offline) may be of secondary importance, although the environment contributes significantly to the manifestation of addictive behaviors
target_learners: adolescents with problematic Internet, smartphone, or social media use
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms behind development and maintenance of addictive online behaviors
examples: The review cites two meta-analyses on Internet Gaming Disorder reporting frontostriatal and fronto-cingulate abnormalities as in line with I-PACE assumptions
key_sources: Marciano Laura, Camerini Anne-Linda, Morese Rosalba. (2021). The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.671817

article_title: Does Instruction-First or Problem-Solving-First Depend on Learners’ Prior Knowledge?
citation: Cheng-Wen He, Logan Fiorella, Paula P. Lemons. (2025). Does Instruction-First or Problem-Solving-First Depend on Learners' Prior Knowledge? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09993-3
title: Competing theoretical accounts: cognitive load theory versus productive failure for instructional sequencing
description: The article frames the instructional-sequence debate through two named accounts. Cognitive load theory posits that "instruction should avoid overloading the capacity of students' limited working memory", predicting I-PS benefits novices and weakens as expertise grows (the expertise reversal effect). Productive failure is "a specific form of PS-I in which the experience of failure during an initial problem-solving phase prepares students to benefit more from subsequent instruction", activating prior knowledge and revealing knowledge gaps. The two experiments were designed to test these competing hypotheses.
requirements: The problem-solving phase in PS-I must be followed by explicit instruction that consolidates learning, per the productive failure guidelines the article cites
constraints: The article notes existing evidence for the moderation is limited and based largely on cross-study comparisons rather than controlled experiments using the same materials
target_learning_goals: understanding the causal mechanisms of noncovalent interactions
near- and far-transfer problem-solving in biochemistry
examples: Experiment 1 tested the productive failure hypothesis with introductory biology students; Experiment 2 tested the cognitive load hypothesis with biochemistry students using identical materials
key_sources: Cheng-Wen He, Logan Fiorella, Paula P. Lemons. (2025). Does Instruction-First or Problem-Solving-First Depend on Learners' Prior Knowledge? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09993-3

article_title: Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment
citation: O'Neill, E. J., Fulton, C., Matthews, J., & Hensey, C. (2026). Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10574-y
title: I-SEE learning strategies: Introducing, Signposting, Enabling and Evaluating organized as recursive quadrants of the framework
description: The framework groups its learning resources and supports into four overarching I-SEE learning strategies delivered predominantly asynchronously online via the VLE: "we broadly grouped the learning resources and supports outlined within the Metacognition Design Framework into four overarching 'I-SEE' learning strategies". Introducing builds metacognitive knowledge through resources and teaching; Signposting communicates expectations via guidance, rubrics and exemplars; Enabling lets students plan, monitor and assess learning through quizzes, checklists and reusable learning objects; Evaluating uses feedback in varied formats so students learn to assess progress and adjust approaches. Though presented sequentially, the strategies are applied collectively as recursive elements throughout the learning journey, depicted as interlocking quadrants of a jigsaw cog.
requirements: Provision of appropriate opportunities for students to practice planning, monitoring and assessing in context
Scaffolding of tasks and dialogue around learning, supported by the VLE
constraints: Strategies are predominantly delivered asynchronously online using the VLE
target_learners: university students in blended or online modules
examples: Quizzes, checklists and reusable learning objects enable planning and monitoring; automated formative, peer and educator feedback support evaluating
key_sources: O'Neill, E. J., Fulton, C., Matthews, J., & Hensey, C. (2026). Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10574-y

article_title: Is ultrasound training sustainable? A systematic review of competency retention in healthcare trainees.
citation: Wang L‐W, Liu C‐H, Li W‐Y, Chiang W‐C, Chiu Y‐L, Ma M H‐M, Chen H‐L, Yang C‐W. (2025). Is ultrasound training sustainable? A systematic review of competency retention in healthcare trainees. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.15751
title: I-AIM framework for organizing and assessing PoCUS competency
description: The Indication–Acquisition–Interpretation–Medical decision-making framework is a mnemonic checklist organizing focused sonography into four steps: "determining appropriate clinical indications and medical necessity", "acquiring high‐quality images", "systematically interpreting sonographic findings", and "integrating these findings into clinical decision‐making". This review uses it as the organizing axis for classifying assessment outcomes and analyzing retention patterns across PoCUS educational interventions.
requirements: Applicable to PoCUS training and assessment across clinical settings such as cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, vascular and procedural interventions
constraints: The review notes few studies have rigorously evaluated the framework's validity and reliability, and the less-explored domains (Acquisition, Indication, Medical decision-making) lack standardized assessment tools
target_learners: healthcare professional trainees: physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, nurse practitioners, paramedics
target_learning_goals: point-of-care ultrasound competency across indication, acquisition, interpretation and medical decision-making domains
key_sources: Wang L‐W, Liu C‐H, Li W‐Y, Chiang W‐C, Chiu Y‐L, Ma M H‐M, Chen H‐L, Yang C‐W. (2025). Is ultrasound training sustainable? A systematic review of competency retention in healthcare trainees. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.15751

article_title: Self-Regulation for Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders: Preliminary Effects of the "I Control" Curriculum
citation: Stephen W. Smith, Ann P. Daunic, James Algina, Donna L. Pitts, Kristen L. Merrill, Michelle M. Cumming, and Courtney Allen. (2017). Self-Regulation for Students With Emotional and Behavioral Disorders: Preliminary Effects of the I Control Curriculum. Journal of Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/1063426616661702
title: I Control curriculum with Brain Training Lab for middle school students with significant behavior problems
description: I Control is a yearlong self-regulation curriculum for middle school students with significant behavior problems in self-contained and alternative settings. Per the article, it is "a yearlong program with four units of instruction in SR (i.e., introduction to EF, goal setting, emotion regulation, SPS) and computerized games to directly train EF skills." It comprises 46 scripted lessons of about 30 minutes delivered twice weekly, plus the Brain Training Lab, a set of computerized games giving students 20 to 30 minutes of weekly direct training of working memory, cognitive shift, and inhibitory control. Lessons combine direct instruction, teacher modeling, guided practice through role-plays and journaling, and independent practice, concluding with six booster lessons for generalization.
requirements: Delivered as self-contained whole group instruction at two lessons per week, with teachers receiving a 2-day, 12-hr workshop and a 1-day refresher session
constraints: Observed implementation fidelity averaged 81% across teachers, and lessons ranged from 15 to 39 min with an average of 26.5 min, indicating variable pacing across classrooms
target_learners: Middle school students with significant emotional and behavioral problems in self-contained and alternative settings
examples: In the pilot, 17 classrooms in four North Florida school districts were randomly assigned to I Control or business-as-usual, with 152 consenting students analyzed in Mplus
key_sources: Stephen W. Smith, Ann P. Daunic, James Algina, Donna L. Pitts, Kristen L. Merrill, Michelle M. Cumming, and Courtney Allen. (2017). Self-Regulation for Students With Emotional and Behavioral Disorders: Preliminary Effects of the I Control Curriculum. Journal of Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/1063426616661702

article_title: Evaluating Student Communication Skills in a Simulation Setting: A Trends Analysis.
citation: Tiwari Tamanna, Nowak Holly, Russell Tanya, Albino Austin, Rivera William, Tobey Tamara, Dye Bruce A. (2025). Evaluating Student Communication Skills in a Simulation Setting: A Trends Analysis. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70042
title: I-ACT (Interprofessional Anschutz Communication Skills Toolbox) standardized patient assessment instrument
description: The I-ACT toolbox is a 15-question instrument established by CAPE in 2015 to assess healthcare students' communication skills. SPs score each question on "a scale of 1.0 (Yes), 0.5 (Partial), and 0.0 (No)," and questions map to six performance domains plus a global item, covering greeting, agenda setting, information gathering and sharing, structure, relationship, and closing.
requirements: SPs trained to portray patient cases and score student performance using the I-ACT scale after each 15-minute encounter
constraints: Assesses communication in simulated encounters, which the authors note "may not fully capture the complexities of real-world patient interactions"
examples: Used as a summative assessment of communication skills in SP encounters at the University of Colorado School of Dental Medicine
key_sources: Tiwari Tamanna, Nowak Holly, Russell Tanya, Albino Austin, Rivera William, Tobey Tamara, Dye Bruce A. (2025). Evaluating Student Communication Skills in a Simulation Setting: A Trends Analysis. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70042
